clue.text: 8 Across I'm excited to take on in general

parts.note: Nap is a card game, so it answers the cross-reference.
Olé! — the shout you let out when excitement takes over.
What the build takes on is ON itself, tacked on the end.

explanation.walkthrough: Paul's joke is circular: the card game nap is named after the very man you are assembling, so the wordplay and the definition point at one person.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example — Bonaparte is the commander a solver reaches for first when a clue says 'general'.

clue.text: Reportedly, celebrity out of work

parts.note: an idol is a celebrity

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' is the soundalike flag. The trap is that the spoken word is a noun and the written one an adjective, so nothing about the surface prepares you for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The sense used of a plant standing unused or hands laid off, not laziness of temperament.

clue.text: Female agent in support of players' association was dithering

parts.note: The Football Association, the players' governing body.
F is the standard abbreviation for female.
A fed is a federal agent.

explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'in support of' means underneath: whatever supports the FA is written below it. Read across the answer and the three fragments come out in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: To faff is to bustle about achieving nothing, which is what dithering looks like from the outside — British colloquial.

clue.text: Commentator's anticipated error — those hanging on by a neck?

definitions.text: those hanging on by a neck?

parts.note: 'due' means anticipated
a lapse is an error

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a racing commentator calling a photo finish, which is why 'by a neck' sits there so innocently.
explanation.definitionFit: A dewlap is the loose fold of skin that dangles from the throat of cattle, dogs and lizards.

clue.text: Partying, where piano found in skip?

parts.note: Piano is P, and in SKIP the P comes after — après is French for after.
The three letters the P follows.

explanation.walkthrough: Piano = P is a music-page convention worth banking, and the question mark admits the rest: this clue reads a word as a map of where its letters sit.
explanation.definitionFit: Après-ski is the drinking and dancing that fills the evening after a day on the slopes, so 'Partying' names the whole scene.

clue.text: A stitch bandaged by beauty, community professional

parts.note: A corker is a beauty — an absolute stunner.
The clue's own A, taken at face value.
To stitch is to sew.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bandaged' keeps the surface medical while quietly doing container duty, and CORKER for beauty is the sort of dated slang Paul keeps in circulation.
explanation.definitionFit: A caseworker is the social-services worker assigned to individual cases, so the definition names the job by where it is done.

clue.text: Tool with key finally locked in dilapidated chest

parts.note: Five of the six letters, straight from the clue.
The last letter of KEY.

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is really put inside anything: 'locked in' only tells you the Y joins the other letters before 'dilapidated' rearranges the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A scythe is the long curved blade for mowing by hand — a tool by category, and the one the Grim Reaper carries.

clue.text: Clown prepared for war, perhaps

parts.note: A card is a joker or a wag — someone who plays the clown.
Game means ready and willing: 'I'm game'.

explanation.walkthrough: This is the puzzle's keystone: half a dozen other clues point back at 8 across, and each of them wants a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: War is one particular card game, so 'perhaps' flags a definition by example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Spot in which I will go fish?

parts.note: A place is a spot.
The clue's I, which goes inside.

explanation.walkthrough: Even the surface stays on theme, since Go Fish is a children's card game. The question mark admits that plaice is one fish rather than a synonym for fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaice is a flatfish, so 'fish?' defines by example, the question mark doing the work of 'for instance'.

clue.text: Red four from sevens or eights

parts.note: Hidden across the join: sevenS OR Eights.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Four from' is the extraction flag — take four letters from what follows — and the card numbers around it are camouflage, not arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflamed skin goes red, which is why 'red raw' and this word describe the same state.

clue.text: London school probing death on the wobbly bridge

definitions.note: A bridge is a single dental fitting, but it is made of more than one false tooth, so a singular definition names a plural answer.

parts.note: Fate is one's doom — death.
The London School of Economics.
THE, made wobbly, comes out as ETH.

explanation.walkthrough: 'The wobbly bridge' is the Millennium Bridge, and it is pure misdirection: the bridge wanted here is the dental one, and death is FATE rather than END.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental bridge is a set of replacement teeth anchored to the real ones — the technical term for the thing itself.

clue.text: Pick up only hearts and diamonds then in snap?

parts.note: To pick something up is to notice or see it.
Hearts and diamonds are the two red suits.

explanation.walkthrough: Snap is a card game and also what a person does on losing their temper; the second sense is the one the answer needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose your temper on the spot is what 'snap' means of a person rather than of a card.

clue.text: Eat greener bananas — and heal

parts.note: The ten letters of EAT GREENER, rearranged.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' is the anagram flag and the surface's fruit at once, which is why a diet clue can sit in a puzzle about cards without looking odd.
explanation.definitionFit: To regenerate tissue is to grow it back, and growing back is exactly what a wound does as it heals.

clue.text: Bridge holiday

definitions.note: 'Bridge' is a verb here and the holiday a noun, so the answer is read as two words for one half of the clue and one word for the other.
definitions.meaning: To bridge a gap means crossing it entirely, skipping whatever lies between.
The Jewish festival of the exodus.

explanation.walkthrough: Two words in the clue, two definitions, no wordplay at all. The theme pushes you towards the card game, which is precisely what the setter is counting on.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridging a gap is passing over it, and the festival is named for the plague that passed over the marked houses.

clue.text: Hopeless at whist, I could get what it is!

definitions.text: Hopeless at whist, I could get what it is!

parts.note: Eight letters, and 'Hopeless' is the instruction to jumble them.
Jumbled, they come out as exactly this phrase — so the clue does the thing it is talking about.

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is its own example. Nothing spells the answer out; you have to notice that one phrase in it rearranges into another, and then name what that trick is called.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: rearrange one phrase in it and out comes another, and the word for that rearrangement is the answer.

clue.text: Budget ultimately invested in a better groomed animal

parts.note: Better groomed is neater, with the clue's own a in front.
The last letter of BUDGET.

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a smarter animal, and the trick is spotting that a two-word comparative is really one word: 'better groomed' equals NEATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A category definition — the setter names the class and leaves you to work out which long-snouted insect eater is meant.

clue.text: Hearts, the first discarded by those not twisting?

parts.note: At pontoon you either twist or stick, so those not twisting are stickers.
The leading S is the letter that goes.

explanation.walkthrough: Twist and stick are pontoon's two calls, so a card-table phrase turns out to be a plain beheading dressed up as gambling nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang from the sound of the organ keeping time — 'a dodgy ticker' — and plural for plural.

clue.text: Preparation for 8 Acrosses, solo and fish

parts.note: A riff is a short solo phrase on a guitar.
The ling is a long-bodied food fish.

explanation.walkthrough: LING is the crossword's workhorse fish and worth memorising. Note the plural cross-reference: 8 across is a whole category, and this clue wants all of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Riffling is the springing shuffle that squares a deck before play, so it is what a card game gets ready with.

clue.text: Drained cups free to be checked

parts.note: Drained of blood — bled.
To rid is to free.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cups' is the container indicator, because to cup something is to hold it — a noun in the surface doing a verb's job in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: To bridle is to rein a horse in, so 'checked' is the restraining sense — held back — rather than the inspecting one.

clue.text: Old maid and spider?

definitions.meaning: The dated term for a woman who never married.
One who spins — which is a spider's whole trade.

explanation.walkthrough: Old Maid and Spider are both card games, so the surface never leaves the theme while both halves of the clue are quietly literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The dated name for an unmarried woman, and older still, one who spins thread — the job a web-maker does.

clue.text: Benefit introducing former network

parts.note: A plus is a benefit.
An ex is a former partner.

explanation.walkthrough: EX for 'former' is a two-letter gift the solver banks for life, and 'introducing' is doing container duty rather than announcing anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plexus is a branching network of nerves or vessels, as in the solar plexus — anatomical rather than everyday.

clue.text: 8 Across blasted, inaccessible?

parts.note: Faro, the old gambling-house card game.
FF is fortissimo — as loud as it will go.

explanation.walkthrough: Every '8 Across' in this puzzle wants a different card game. Note that the wordplay splits four and two while the answer is written three and three.
explanation.definitionFit: Distance standing in for unreachability, the question mark admitting that a long way away is not quite impossible to get to.

clue.text: Poker face in game, better concealing that

parts.note: Better as in finer, of higher quality.
A face is a front, and the front of GAME is G.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Poker face' is one phrase in the surface and two jobs in the parse: the definition takes the first word, the wordplay the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A poker is whatever does the poking — a fire iron, or the thing you prod someone with — so the noun is an agent, not a game.

clue.text: Brag about drinking always, with office in location adjoining pub

parts.note: BRAG keeps its B where it is and turns its RAG about.
E'er is the poets' always.
A den is the room you work in at home.

explanation.walkthrough: Only part of the word turns: the B stays put while its RAG comes back. 'Drinking' does the swallowing and keeps the whole surface in the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The outdoor area attached to a public house, so the definition describes the place by what it sits beside.

clue.text: A little patience, else fish

parts.note: Hidden across the comma: patiencE ELSe.

explanation.walkthrough: Patience is the card game the surface wants you to see, and 'a little' is the standard flag for taking a small piece of what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Snake-like fish by category, and since 'fish' is the same word in the plural it matches the answer's number.

clue.text: Bounce back in elimination contest, hammering opponent firstly

parts.note: The first letter of each of the four words.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Firstly' sits at the end of the clue rather than the front: an instruction may come after the words it operates on, and often does.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound thrown back off a wall, so the definition names it by the physics rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Cheat thus toyed with love, heart surrendered

parts.note: Four of the six letters, straight from the clue.
The word that is about to be trimmed.
The heart of LOVE, its middle pair, is surrendered — leaving LE.

explanation.walkthrough: LOVE gives up its middle before anything is rearranged. 'Toyed with' is the anagram flag and the surface's flirtation at once.
explanation.definitionFit: To hustle is to swindle by fast talk — the pool-hall sense of the word, not the hurrying one.

clue.text: Solo effort's last seen by retiring footballer, giant

parts.note: Pelé, written backwards.
Han Solo, so 'Solo' is a surname here.
The final letter of EFFORT.

explanation.walkthrough: The capital S at the head of the clue hides the Star Wars surname, and Pelé is the footballer every setter reaches for when four letters are wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant of land animals, so the word defines by sheer size — a noun standing in for its biggest example.
